summary: Retrieval-augmented vision-language models (VLMs) answer from two sources of evidence that can each fail: the retrieved text can be wrong or noisy, and the image can be degraded or contradicted. We introduce GIB-200K, 200,000 image-question items built from COCO and Visual Genome, each expanded into controlled stress conditions: hard-negative retrieval noise (1-20 documents), visual ambiguity (Gaussian and motion blur, low-resource crops) and cross-modal conflict with counterfactual flip pairs. Instead of only measuring degradation, we ask how models combine the two modalities. From ideal Bayesian cue combination we derive a testable prediction that yields formal definitions of Knowledge Inertia (text over-weighted relative to the model's own image evidence) and Sensory Capture (the reverse), and we estimate the weights with a measurement-error-corrected regression whose recovery of known weights we verify. A counterfactual flip decomposition separates modality bias from concept priors, and a Grounding Illusion Score measures how much clean accuracy is not grounded in the image. We evaluate 4 open models on one frozen, seeded evaluation split of 2,000 GIB-200K items. All models are accurate on clean inputs (92.5%-94.2%) but adverse accuracy falls to 41.3%-59.9%. The two LLaVA models over-weight the text (Knowledge Inertia, w_T/w_I = 1.229 and 1.322), whereas InternVL3 favours the image (w_T/w_I = 0.680); between 34.8% and 71.4% of the clean answers that are correct are abandoned when the document lies. A training-free consistency check that compares the answer with and without retrieval trades coverage for accuracy under misleading documents, while falling back to the image fails when the image is heavily degraded. All per-instance outputs, code, and an audit that recomputes every reported open-model number are released.
title: The Illusion of Grounding: Do Vision-Language Models Weigh Retrieved Text and Images Like an Ideal Observer?

summary: Unplanned 30-day intensive care unit (ICU) readmission is a critical benchmark for evaluating healthcare quality. Most predictive models assume readmission risk depends solely on a patient's individual pathophysiological state, ignoring hospital operational context and resource capacity. In practice, discharge decisions are dynamic trade-offs between patient stability and bed turnover pressures. To address this gap, we develop an Operation-aware Multimodal Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) for ICU discharge risk assessment. The system combines multi-agent collaborative extraction with self-evolving retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to eliminate template noise from progress notes, while constructing departmental workload indicators alongside admission flow features, continuous vital signs, and sparse medical codes (ICD/DRG). Addressing severe class imbalance (about 10.5% readmissions) and alarm fatigue, we implement data normalization, class reweighting, and decision-threshold calibration. In 20 independent runs across 20,000 ICU stays from MIMIC-III, empirical findings demonstrate that: vital signs alone have limited predictive capacity under real-world class imbalance (PR-AUC of 0.1387 +/- 0.0086); directly concatenating raw text embeddings degrades decision tree performance (XGBoost and LightGBM PR-AUC drop to 0.3893 and 0.4030); whereas an end-to-end multimodal fine-tuning architecture (Transformer E2E FineTune) utilizing layer-wise parameter freezing and differential learning rates reverses text negative transfer, achieving the highest AUROC of 0.8288 +/- 0.0110, PR-AUC of 0.4373 +/- 0.0310, and F1-Score of 0.4757 +/- 0.0196. Operational indicators supply independent risk signals, laying an engineering foundation for high-utility clinical decision support tools.
title: Operation-aware Multimodal Clinical Decision Support System for ICU Discharge Risk Assessment

summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems face security, privacy, and copyright risks including content leakage, source reconstruction, unauthorized access, data poisoning, and prompt injection. Yet RAG protection studies use incompatible evaluation metrics, datasets, and threat models. We present a systematic survey and human-coded evidence map of 118 full-text-confirmed RAG defense papers, organized by measured endpoint rather than claimed goal or defense mechanism. Our seven-family taxonomy covers content disclosure, formal privacy proxies, access control and suppression, corpus-use detection, and pipeline integrity and attribution. Thirty-two annotators double-coded the papers kappa=0.867. The survey identifies three gaps. First, retrieval reranking and context rewriting each span five or six endpoint families, so mechanisms do not identify protection outcomes. Second, only 17.8% of studies use content disclosure or reconstruction as their primary endpoint; under the frozen copyright/ownership relation label, 73.3% of records have corpus-use detection as their primary endpoint, and none have an emitted-expression primary endpoint. Third, most evaluations use general-purpose question-answering datasets and non-adaptive attacks rather than sensitive data and adaptive, multi-turn extraction. Our controlled RAG testbed shows that preventing verbatim copying does not prevent private-fact recovery: a normalized 8-gram guard reduces 20-token copying to 0.0%, but a three-query adaptive attacker recovers 48.3% of hidden facts on Qwen3-8B. We release the taxonomy, dataset, coding protocols, and testbed to enable comparable, claim-aligned RAG security evaluation.
title: Protection Is Not One Event: A Survey of RAG Protection Research by Measured Endpoint

summary: Reproduction package for a measurement study of what static analysis recovers from stripped binaries produced by Nuitka and Cython, two compilers used to package Python programs (including malware that uses them to hinder analysis). It contains the frozen build recipes, the analysis and measurement scripts, the ground-truth construction, the canonical result tables behind every reported number, and the figure scripts, with instructions to rebuild the environment from the listed PyPI packages. No malware and no compiled binaries are included; every build is reproducible from the listed packages.
title: Recovering Python functions from stripped Nuitka and Cython binaries: ground truth and a measurement study (code and results)

summary: Vector search over learned embeddings is the retrieval layer of recommendation and retrieval-augmented generation, and many applications cap how many answer items one category may contribute. Graph indexes answer a query by best-first traversal, and where it stops determines its cost and whether its answer is exact. We study early termination for such constrained $k$-nearest-neighbor ($k$-NN) queries, with plain $k$-NN as a special case, and seek the cheapest stopping rule whose answer is exact with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$. Learned early-termination methods instead target average recall, which does not guarantee exact answers. Multiple testing can calibrate any parameterized stopping rule to our target, but it cannot tell how much a better rule with the same risk and observations would save. Answering this needs a lower bound on the optimum of a rule family too large to enumerate, valid for the query population. Our key idea is to declare the observations a rule may use and to consider every rule monotone in them. Risk-constrained stopping then becomes a linear program over an order polytope, whose Lagrangian minimizers form a nested chain of staircase rules computed exactly by dynamic programming. Fixed-sequence binomial tests along this chain calibrate our rule, CaST, whose failure probability is at most $\varepsilon$ with confidence $1-δ$. Lagrangian weak duality bounds the optimum of the declared class from below at all risk levels at once, without a union bound over the rules. On two datasets of one million items each, CaST replayed on logged searches costs at most 1.132 times the class optimum for risk levels from 0.03 to 0.10, at 95% joint confidence per setting. Larger savings thus need a rule outside the class. At a common risk target on held-out queries, CaST is faster than every other calibrated rule we time, which take 4.8% to 45.5% more mean time.
title: Calibrated Early Termination with Bounded Optimality Gaps for Constrained Vector Search

summary: This study evaluated genetic parameters of raw flesh colour traits in market-size Amur mirror carp and their relationships with key performance traits after the second overwintering and at market size. Flesh colour traits (lightness L*, redness a*, yellowness b* and chroma C*) were measured in 1,277 pedigree-assigned individuals using the CIE Lab system. Heritability estimates were significant and ranged from low to moderate (L* = 0.16, a* = 0.39, b* = 0.23, C* = 0.30), indicating potential for genetic improvement. After the second overwintering, body weight was genetically associated with lower L* (-0.44 ± 0.16) and higher a* (0.43 ± 0.14), while muscle fat content was positively genetically correlated with a* (0.46 ± 0.13), b* (0.48 ± 0.14) and C* (0.58 ± 0.14). At market size, specific growth rate showed strong negative genetic correlations with a* (-0.75 ± 0.08) and C* (-0.64 ± 0.11), but a positive correlation with L* (rg = 0.44). Gonadosomatic index was negatively correlated with L* (rg = -0.65± 0.12; rp = -0.22) and positively with a* (rg = 0.35 ± 0.15, rp = 0.25). These contrasting correlation patterns suggest that estimated genetic relationships between flesh colour and performance may vary with rearing conditions and the relative contribution of natural and supplemental feed as well as changes in fish age, body size, and physiological state. Although flesh colour is heritable, its invasive measurement limits direct application in routine selection. Feeding and pond management may therefore provide more practical approaches for modifying flesh colour, while selective breeding could be considered through family, genomic or indirect selection strategies.
title: Genetic parameters of raw flesh colour traits in Amur mirror carp and their relation to performance traits

summary: Dexterous hand design demands repeated expert work across geometry, robot-description code, collision debugging, grasp initialization, and policy training. We present Task2Hand, a Skill: a specification package that turns a functional manipulation brief into a parameterized hand model and routes every candidate through cost-ordered contact, dynamics, and learning gates. Each gate returns a status and an evidence record; on failure, the Skill records the earliest blocker, revises one bounded parameter group, and reruns the cheaper gates. The agent generates, validates, and trains autonomously within declared bounds, and escalates trade-offs, plateaus, and conflicting evidence to a human who sets the next design direction. An evidence-driven design trajectory for bidirectional in-hand manipulation yielded SAGE Hand (Skill-Aware Generative Embodiment): four fingers, 16 actuated DoF, an integrated guiding palm, compact roots, cylindrical tips, and a collision-cleared opposable thumb. Under a matched training protocol, SAGE Hand reaches 45.6% task success on a hexagonal prism against 37.3% for the LEAP hand, and 70.8% on a bicolor cylinder against 51.6%. Dense simulated tactile input more than halves the cylinder drop rate. In a controlled iteration study, the Skill path preserves capture at 164/165 trials while the path without the Skill degrades to 14/165, confirming that the gates act as a regression guard during refinement. Accepted candidates pack with URDF/MJCF, metrics, checkpoints, and a provenance manifest.
title: Task2Hand: A Contact-Grounded Skill for Parametric Dexterous-Hand Morphology Design

summary: Fault Detection and Diagnosis (FDD) is crucial for both maintenance and control in chemical industries, where early fault detection can prevent costly failures and optimize operations. This is particularly critical in pilot units like those at IFP Energies Nouvelles (IFPEN), which operate under short-term experimental conditions with frequently varying operational parameters. This study conducts an extensive benchmarking analysis using the Tennessee Eastman Process (TEP), a widely used simulated chemical process dataset, to evaluate multiple approaches for fault detection and diagnosis, featuring numerous continuous operations with different sensors and faults. Several methods were implemented and compared including Multi Scale PCA (MS-PCA), AutoEncoder, Ensemble Learning, and LSTM models for fault detection, alongside Random Forest, XGBoost, and BLSTM (Bidirectional LSTM) for fault diagnosis. Our results demonstrate that Ensemble Learning achieves detection rates ranging from 80% to 100% across various fault scenarios. For the fault diagnosis task, BLSTM achieved a diagnosis accuracy of 98.76%. The study reveals that ensemble-based approaches consistently outperform individual models in handling the complex, multivariate nature of chemical process data, due to its robustness in combining multiple perspectives, comprehensive data capture, and localized detection capabilities. Furthermore, the superior performance of the BLSTM is due to its ability to capture both past and future temporal dependencies in the sequential data, particularly important in chemical processes where fault patterns may manifest with complex temporal relationships. This research contributes to the field of Fault Detection and Diagnosis by providing empirical evidence for the effectiveness of ensemble methods and Bidirectional LSTMs in order to address industrial FDD applications on chemical processes.
title: Comparative Performance of Machine Learning Architectures for Fault Detection and Diagnosis in Chemical Processes

summary: Reward-independent representations enable reinforcement learning agents to reuse knowledge across tasks, but limited representation capacity raises three fundamental questions: what statistical dependence should these representations capture, which components of that dependence should be retained for policy improvement, and how does discarding the remaining components affect decision-making? We address these questions through canonical dependence analysis. For a reference policy, we construct an action-centered, positive-lag canonical dependence matrix (CDM) that isolates the additional predictive contribution of the current action beyond the current state. Its singular value decomposition yields Spectral Universal Advantage Features (SUAF), paired features that recover delayed advantage through linear reward projections. We show that the spectrum quantifies mutual information between current action and future state-action visitation conditioned on current state and determines reward specific approximation errors. Retaining the leading modes gives optimal rank-constrained approximations under both isotropic average-case and reward-uniform minimax criteria. Separating the immediate reward contrast also avoids the spectral floor arising from direct compression of the full advantage operator. To learn SUAF from reward-free data, we develop an action-centered Soft-HGR objective with bidirectional temporal-difference estimation. We further connect spectral approximation errors to sufficient conditions for policy improvement. Finite-state experiments validate the spectral predictions and feature-learning method, while zero-shot evaluations on discrete tasks and continuous-control benchmarks demonstrate the utility of the learned representations across rewards.
title: SUAF: Spectral Universal Advantage Features for Zero-Shot Policy Improvement

summary: Abstract (it) Il corpus in esame decostruisce il mito dell’applicazione standardizzata della prospettiva albertiana basata su una griglia di quadrati nell’opera di Leonardo da Vinci, proponendo un paradigma metrico-modulare fondato su evidenze geometriche oggettive e falsificabili. Attraverso l’analisi tridimensionale dell’Annunciazione, dell’Adorazione dei Magi e dell’Ultima Cena, emerge una grammatica spaziale in costante evoluzione. Leonardo abbandona la rigida scacchiera per sviluppare un sistema di “righelli inseriti”, evolvendo da una misurazione monodirezionale a un’architettura ritmica e stereometrica. Il metodo d’indagine, basato su tecniche di retroingegneria CAD e sul “banale aristotelico”, dimostra come le proporzioni spaziali (dalla proporzione 3:1:3, passando per il modulo 4:3, il rapporto 1:4 e gli angoli a 36° fino ad arrivare ai ritmi polifonici 1:4:1, 2:1:2 e 1:6:1) siano direttamente ricavabili dall’opera stessa. Riferimento teorico primario del corpus è il Manoscritto A di Leonardo (f. 41r), secondo cui la profondità dello spazio dipinto si costruisce da riduzioni misurabili, prima ancora che da una griglia di quadrati. L’approccio restituisce spazi non solo misurabili, ma architettonicamente rimontabili e strutturati sulle misure umane, rigettando interpretazioni esoteriche o simbologie forzate. Abstract (en) The examined corpus deconstructs the myth of the standardized application of Albertian perspective based on a grid of squares in the works of Leonardo da Vinci, proposing a metric-modular paradigm founded on objective and falsifiable geometric evidence. Through the three-dimensional analysis of the Annunciation, the Adoration of the Magi, and the Last Supper, a constantly evolving spatial grammar emerges. Leonardo abandons the rigid checkerboard to develop a system of “inserted rulers,” evolving from a monodirectional measurement to a rhythmic and stereometric architecture. The investigative method, based on CAD reverse-engineering techniques and the “Aristotelian obvious,” demonstrates how spatial proportions (from the 3:1:3 proportion, passing through the 4:3 module, the 1:4 ratio and the 36° angles, up to the 1:4:1, 2:1:2 and 1:6:1 polyphonic rhythms) can be directly derived from the artwork itself. The primary theoretical reference of the corpus is Leonardo’s Manuscript A (f. 41r), according to which the depth of painted space is constructed from measurable reductions, even before a grid of squares. This approach yields spaces that are not only measurable but architecturally reassemblable and structured on human measurements, rejecting esoteric interpretations or forced symbolism. Abstract esteso (IT) Il corpus Leonardo's CAD, Leonardo's Rulers, Leonardo's Score propone una rilettura unitaria di tre indagini nate separatamente ma convergenti verso una stessa ipotesi: Leonardo da Vinci non applica in modo meccanico la prospettiva albertiana a maglia quadrata, né se ne discosta episodicamente per errore o licenza, ma sviluppa progressivamente una propria grammatica spaziale metrico-modulare, verificabile a partire dall'immagine stessa. L'oggetto della ricerca non è una lettura iconografica complessiva delle opere, bensì la ricostruzione degli spazi dipinti come dispositivi misurabili, abitabili e rimontabili attraverso procedure geometriche esplicite. Il trittico mette in relazione tre momenti distinti di questa elaborazione: l’ Annunciazione come forma prototipica della “geometria inserita”, l’ Adorazione dei Magi come emersione di una griglia generativa 4:3 connessa al braccio fiorentino, e l’ Ultima Cena come approdo a una vera polifonia stereometrica, governata da un unico modulo capace di coordinare larghezza, altezza e profondità. In questa prospettiva, lo sviluppo dell’opera leonardesca appare co
title: Leonardo's Spatial Grammar: A CAD Reverse-Engineering Analysis Corpus: Leonardo's CAD, Leonardo's Rulers, Leonardo's Score

summary: We prove optimal non-uniqueness of Leray solutions of the unforced incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in 3D within the class of axially symmetric swirl-free flows. More precisely, we construct two solutions $u_1,u_2$ that have the same initial data $u_1(0)=u_2(0)$, are smooth for every positive time, satisfy the energy identity, and satisfy \[ u_1,u_2\in C_tH_x^α\cap L_t^2H_x^{α+1}\,\,\text{ for every }\,\,0\leqα<1/2,\qquad u_1,u_2\in L_t^\infty L_x^{3,\infty}\cap L_t^{2,\infty}L_x^\infty. \] Thus non-uniqueness holds in optimal Sobolev spaces and critical Ladyzhenskaya-Prodi-Serrin weak spaces, even in a symmetry class where smooth solutions are globally regular. The proof relies on a computer-assisted construction of a linearly unstable forward self-similar solution, starting from the numerical profiles identified in our preceding paper (arXiv:2606.07501). We combine explicit asymptotic expansions and global residual estimates with weak coercivity inequalities stabilized by finitely many functionals. Approximate solutions of auxiliary linear equations yield quantitative inverse bounds, allowing us to correct both the stationary profile and its unstable eigenpair by contraction arguments. The instability and localization theorem proved in arXiv:2606.07501 then produces the non-unique solutions.
title: On the non-uniqueness of solutions of the axi-symmetric swirl-free Navier-Stokes equations, II

summary: For an absorbed one-dimensional diffusion, we characterize two-point restart laws preserving the exit-side probability for every independent renewal clock. Spectral identities establish rigidity under spatial accumulation, while explicit nonsymmetric potentials admit neutral pairs. We distinguish midpoint Dirichlet isospectrality from Weyl reflection rigidity and prove a second-order high-energy asymptotic under local continuity, giving two necessary asymmetry conditions for neutral pairs. Two complete exit profiles at distinct reset rates identify diffusivity and drift; a finite birth-death analogue admits exact Jacobi criteria and reconstruction from four channel functions.
title: Exit-Pair Rigidity, Neutral Restart Laws, and Inverse Reconstruction in One Dimension

summary: We develop a method for forming Ramsey fringes in atomic interferometers as a difference error signal using the phase-jump technique for Ramsey pulses (phase-jump error signal). In this case, the measurement procedure can be implemented as stabilization (locking) of the frequency chirp rate at the central zero of the error signal. We show analytically that this approach allows suppressing the lineshape-asymmetry-caused shift (LACS). This shift was recently theoretically predicted and experimentally identified in the papers [V. I. Yudin et al., JETP Lett. \textbf{122}, 737 (2025); D. N. Kapusta et al., JETP Lett. \textbf{123}, 388 (2026)]. A characteristic feature of the LACS is an inverse cubic dependence $\propto 1/T^3$ (where $T$ is the time between adjacent Ramsey pulses), and it can become dominant for interferometers with a short baseline. Therefore, the developed measurement algorithm with a phase-jump error signal will enable significant improvement in the metrological performance of compact quantum sensors for various purposes (atomic gravimeters, accelerometers, gyroscopes).
title: Atomic interferometry based on a phase-jump error signal with suppression of the lineshape-asymmetry-caused shift

summary: Existing no-reference point cloud quality assessment (NR-PCQA) methods perform well within individual datasets but generalize poorly across datasets. We identify insufficient distortion coverage in training data as a key cause: on unseen distortion types, models rank severity levels near chance or even in reverse. We propose perceptually gated synthetic supervision for no-reference point cloud quality assessment (PGS-PCQA), an NR-PCQA model trained with synthetic distortion ranking. It builds a synthetic distortion bank from source reference point clouds and uses within-type severity ranking as supervision in addition to the source mean opinion scores (MOS), requiring no subjective scores for the synthetic samples. Since higher severity does not always mean lower perceived quality, a perceptual gate softens the ranking targets of pairs with small perceptual differences in rendered views. The synthetic supervision is used only during training and needs no target-domain data. In a single training run on SJTU-PCQA, PGS-PCQA achieves Spearman rank correlation coefficients (SRCCs) of 0.709 on WPC and 0.751 on BASICS. The corresponding published DSP-PCQA scores are 0.595 and 0.723. Under reference-disjoint cross-validation, PGS-PCQA achieves SRCCs of 0.955 on SJTU-PCQA, 0.934 on WPC, 0.906 on BASICS, and 0.791 on LS-PCQA Part I. In the exclusion experiment, the reported scores for the reduced synthetic bank represent 58-65% of the full-bank SRCC gain relative to training without the bank. Code is available at https://github.com/Fan-QY/PGS-PCQA.
title: PGS-PCQA: Perceptually Gated Synthetic Supervision for No-Reference Point Cloud Quality Assessment

summary: The excited-state properties of imide-based defect double antiperovskites AE$_5$AsPn(NH)$_2$ (AE = Ca, Sr; Pn = Sb, Bi) are investigated using spin--orbit-coupled quasiparticle calculations, the model Bethe--Salpeter equation (mBSE), and analytical descriptions of lattice-polarization effects. Across five tetragonal ($P4/mmm$) and monoclinic ($Cm$) structural models, the calculated exciton binding energies range from 140 to 210 meV. Chemical substitution modifies both the binding energies and the hydrogenic estimates of exciton spatial extent. By contrast, the structural distortion from tetragonal $P4/mmm$ ($D_{4h}$) to monoclinic $Cm$ ($C_s$), which removes inversion and fourfold rotational symmetry, produces comparatively modest changes in binding energy but appreciably reshapes the real- and momentum-space exciton distributions. This contrast reveals a partial decoupling between exciton energetics and wavefunction geometry, and identifies a symmetry-associated sensitivity of exciton geometry to structural distortion. The changes are understood to occur together with modifications of local coordination and electronic dispersion, rather than as an isolated effect of symmetry alone. Lattice polarization provides an additional screening channel, reducing the estimated exciton binding energies by approximately 9--16\%. Complementary Fröhlich-polaron calculations yield moderate mass enhancement and model-estimated electron-polaron mobilities of 39--99 cm$^2$ V$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$, with comparatively modest differences between the two polymorphs. These results highlight the distinct responses of exciton energetics, exciton wavefunction geometry, and carrier transport to chemical and structural modifications.
title: Decoupling Exciton Energetics from Wavefunction Geometry in Imide-Based Defect Double Antiperovskites

summary: Constructing an effective low-dimensional stochastic model from sparse observations requires separating deterministic drift from state-dependent fluctuations when the governing interaction law is unknown. We formulate an adaptive neural stochastic differential equation with topology constraints (TC-AdaNSDE) for two-variable predator--prey dynamics. To regularize the inverse problem when data are scarce, the model combines flexible drift and correlated diffusion fields with density-adaptive local Kramers--Moyal moment estimates and soft phase-space constraints reflecting boundary saddle behavior near extinction and local stability near coexistence. Using a known nonlinear stochastic system, we first show that short-time trajectory error cannot assess diffusion accuracy on its own and must be paired with distributional measures of one-step transitions and long-time phase-space occupancy. We then apply this framework to macroscopic turbulence and zonal flow energies reduced from Hasegawa--Wakatani plasma simulations and to short ecological time series. In the sparse-data regime, TC-AdaNSDE reproduces both short-horizon evolution and long-time invariant energy distributions where deterministic reductions collapse and unconstrained stochastic fits diverge, while recovering physically interpretable drift and fluctuation fields across both physical and biological systems.
title: Learning effective stochastic predator and prey dynamics across physical and biological systems from limited data

summary: Recent studies have identified orbital exchange fields as a novel mechanism for controlling electronic and magnetic phenomena through the orbital degree of freedom. In contrast to conventional spin exchange fields, orbital exchange fields couple directly to orbital angular momentum and can emerge from purely orbital interactions or dynamically through couplings to chiral excitations such as phonons and magnons. Motivated by these developments, we investigate the transport and torque responses generated by orbital exchange fields in two-dimensional materials. Using monolayer H-phase MoS$_2$ as a prototypical transition-metal dichalcogenide, we introduce a Zeeman-like orbital exchange field that breaks time-reversal symmetry in orbital space while leaving the spin degree of freedom inactive. We demonstrate that this perturbation induces a sizable intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivity even in the absence of spin magnetism and spin--orbit coupling driven mechanisms. Simultaneously, the orbital Hall response remains robust in the weak-field regime and undergoes substantial reconstruction at larger exchange strengths due to pronounced band modifications. In addition, we show that currents can generate sizable current-induced orbital torques on the orbital magnetization. Our results establish orbital exchange fields as an effective route toward Hall transport and nonequilibrium torque phenomena driven purely by orbital physics, opening new perspectives for orbitronics and orbitally engineered quantum functionalities.
title: Pure Orbitronics: Hall Responses and Torques by Orbital Exchange in Spinless Transition-Metal Dichalcogenides

summary: Frustrated magnets on triangular lattices favour noncollinear order, and when inversion symmetry is broken they can host localized topological textures on top of that order. Here we show that the Janus MXene MnHf2C2FI is such a system. Combining first-principles calculations with atomistic spin simulations, we find that magnetism is confined to the Mn layer, where a strong antiferromagnetic nearest-neighbor exchange together with a sizable Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction stabilizes a frustrated 120 Neel ground state. On top of this ground state we identify a metastable hexameron: a composite of six merons and antimerons, one vortex-antivortex pair on each of the three sublattices, whose sublattice-resolved topological charges compensate. Linear spin-wave theory confirms that the hexameron is a local energy minimum, and its noncoplanar cores act as potential wells that bind discrete in-gap magnon modes below the bulk continuum. In a periodic hexameron array the magnon bands carry nonzero Chern numbers, and the resulting Berry curvature produces a magnon thermal Hall response whose sign depends on which of the two time-reversal partners of the hexameron is realized. Our results establish Janus MXenes as a two-dimensional platform in which frustration, broken inversion symmetry, and spin-orbit coupling combine to produce metastable antiferromagnetic solitons with distinct spectroscopic and transport fingerprints.
title: Frustration-Stabilized Hexamerons and Their Topological Magnons in Janus MXene

summary: Abstract This integrative research synthesis develops a candidate relational architecture across quantum foundations, physical history, persistent organization, relational time, and the recovery problem for spacetime. Its method is unification by decomposition : constraint, weighting, singular factualization, and retention are treated as distinct operations with distinct evidential burdens. Key Analyses & Framework Quantum Foundations & Entanglement: The double slit separates coherent alternatives, receiver-defined effects, Born weighting, and the $n = 1$ record. The Sorkin hierarchy and reconstruction literature delimit what is already formally known and leave open the physical motivation for second-order weighting. Entanglement is analyzed through a missing-loss audit: spatial routing, operational differentiation, and dynamical decoupling do not by themselves demonstrate ontological severance of a nonfactorizable joint state. Ontology & Event-Factualization: Primitive factualization is treated as a technical event-ontology posit, with fundamental agency as a stronger interpretive hypothesis (alongside objective stochasticity, Bohmian completion, Everettian branching, and collapse dynamics as comparison classes). A present-state coherence veto prevents absolute factualization while coherence-bearing degrees of freedom remain causally accessible to future interactions in which their phase relation can again matter. Retained factual consequences provide the bridge to physical history, memory, differential persistence, and increasingly organized agency. Downstream Physics & Empirical Testing: Transition and stabilization are treated as relational roles of one field-energy reality rather than new substances. The synthesis incorporates a fully exposed prospective transition-stabilization kill test in a driven liquid-to-vapor system and preserves planetary, gravitational, and spacetime extensions as explicitly conditional research branches. Methodological Stance: No universal master equation is claimed. The program is a structured ontology, audit, and research architecture whose modules must earn mathematical or empirical closure independently. Philosophical Extensions (Dual-Aspect Hypothesis): A further dual-aspect factualist hypothesis, with a panexperiential extension, distinguishes the publicly accessible objective face of factual processes from a minimally subjective first-person-like aspect associated with irreducible factual resolution. This is presented as a stronger ontological interpretation, not as an experimentally established consequence. It does not identify an elementary subjective aspect with a subject, mind, or consciousness. Complex biological agency is treated as potentially nested and hierarchically integrated, while the combination of elementary subjective loci into a unified subject is left as an explicit unresolved problem.
title: Unification by Decomposition: The Dualverse — From Quantum Factualization and Physical Memory to Hierarchical Individuality and Spacetime

summary: This repository provides supporting research code for the manuscript "LoRA-Based Diffusion Data Augmentation for Underwater Garbage Detection: An Empirical Study with YOLOv8s", submitted to Scientific Reports. The study investigates whether class-specific Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) provides additional benefits over ControlNet-conditioned synthetic data augmentation for underwater garbage detection using YOLOv8s. The archive includes selected Python source code for paired synthetic-image generation workflows, data and annotation quality assurance, detector-training controls, validation procedures, and exploratory Kernel Inception Distance (KID) analysis. The experiments use a frozen grouped dataset partition with 3,566 training images, 997 validation images, 471 test images, and 96 excluded images. The full-data comparison evaluates real-only training (A), ControlNet-only augmentation (E), and ControlNet-plus-LoRA augmentation (F) using five matched detector seeds. A separate 50%-training-data sensitivity analysis is evaluated on the validation set only. The released archive contains supporting code, configuration information, integrity checksums, and selected aggregate results. Original datasets, model checkpoints, and some historical execution records are not redistributed. Certain historical code versions have unresolved provenance, and the archive does not constitute a fully verified, one-command reproduction of the complete experiments. The experimental findings do not establish a consistent incremental detection benefit from LoRA over matched ControlNet-only augmentation.
title: Supporting Code for LoRA-Based Diffusion Data Augmentation for Underwater Garbage Detection

summary: This dataset brings together five open data sources to study how users of Indonesian mobile telemedicine apps infer whether a human doctor or an automated agent is answering them, and how that perceived source attribution relates to trust and to the place of human care. It combines Google Play reviews of four telemedicine apps (Alodokter, Halodoc, KlikDokter, YesDok), expert-labelled doctor answers from Alodokter, interview quotes from generative-AI users, national context indicators from the World Bank, and generative-AI-era app reviews. No data were collected from scratch: every row is a coded extract of an openly licensed source, and the provenance of each row is recorded. The sources are kept in separate sheets by design: user reviews, doctors' messages and AI-user interviews offer three vantage points on the same phenomenon, and interpretation should remain tied to each source (comparison at the level of constructs, not pooled records). The sources also cover different periods, so differences between them may reflect time as well as vantage point. The workbook contains a README sheet, a source register with SHA-256 checksums, five coded data sheets, a codebook, value labels and a reliability record. Six sheets document the researchers' validation codes, recoding checks and reconciliation decisions, and seven further sheets report the blind post-revision holdout, the explicit or implicit classification of human attributions, agreement per category with bootstrap intervals, confusion matrices, the trust tables with and without platform-related reviews, and the coding of message cues that links the reviews to the doctor answers. Each sheet is also provided as a UTF-8 CSV file, together with five Python analysis scripts and the JASP 0.99.0 outputs that replicate the main estimates. The researchers set the codebook, categories, and keyword rules from the study's theoretical framework. An AI tool (Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic) was used only to apply that codebook in an initial labelling pass over Sources A and E. Reliability was examined in three steps. First, two researchers independently coded a stratified random sample of 100 Source A reviews without seeing the initial labels; before reconciliation they agreed on relevance for 98 reviews (κ = .79, bootstrap 95% CI .38 to 1.00, a prevalence effect; PABAK = .96) and, on the 94 reviews both judged relevant, κ = .93 for source attribution, .90 for trust basis and 1.00 for trust direction. The initial AI-assisted labels agreed poorly with the researchers (κ = .12 to .53) because two definitions had been read more narrowly, so the researchers' judgement was taken as the reference standard and the codebook was revised (relevance now covers platform communication; HUMAN_AFFIRMED now covers implicit attribution to the app's doctor). Second, all 1,248 Source A reviews were recoded under the revised rules and every changed row was checked by a researcher (352 rows on relevance, 7 corrected; 245 rows on attribution, 18 corrected); this check was not blind. Third, both researchers coded a fresh stratified holdout of 113 Source A reviews blind to the final codes and to each other, with rare categories oversampled: κ = .83 (.73 to .91) for source attribution, .86 (.78 to .93) for trust basis, .87 (.78 to .94) for trust direction and .78 for explicit versus implicit human attribution. summary: Long-context models use sparse or structured attention to avoid quadratic cost, yet retrieving a small set of relevant facts embedded among hundreds of thousands of distractors degrades as normalization mass disperses with length. Hub-and-spoke optimal transport (OT) replaces the dense $L \times L$ matrix with a linear-size graph over local windows and $K$ shared hubs balanced by Sinkhorn scaling. Building on block-wise tail refinement and fixed-support transport topology (arXiv:2605.08123, arXiv:2609.07954), we introduce Topology Hub Optimal Transport (THOT): (1) bounded-support capacity gating via simplex sparsemax ($O(L\log L)$) or sorting-free token-local thresholded ReLU ($O(L)$), driving excess distractor mass to zero; (2) a three-sweep $1+2$ annealed row-closed Sinkhorn schedule that damps bipartite residuals; (3) an exact rank-$(D+2R+1)$ One-Reference-Tile adjoint in batched split-factor Triton kernels (BF16 Tensor Cores, FP32 potentials); and (4) a chunked exclusive-prefix causal variant with verified zero future leakage. On NVIDIA L4, sparsemax THOT trained at $L=128$ reaches 97.40% zero-shot recall of fixed bindings at $L=262{,}144$ under pure task loss ($α=0$) and 98.83% at $α=0.05$ (matched by $O(L)$ thresholded ReLU at $α=0.05$, vs. 80.60% at $α=0$), while softmax-gated hub OT drops to 3.52%. In bidirectional operator microbenchmarks, our kernel runs forward+VJP in 100.1 ms at $H=8, D=64, L=262\mathrm{K}$ (2.2x faster with 4.0x smaller compiler temporaries than latent softmax) and 1.34 ms vs. 4.37 ms for cuDNN FlashAttention at $L=4{,}096$; multi-layer LM runs use the unfused path. summary: The work continues the geometric model of the distribution of primes [2] and the work “The Number Arrow and the Line 1/2” [1]. The geometric formula for the number of odd composites up to p², N(p) = 1 + 3(p − 1)(p − 3)/8, is treated as the first level of a ladder in which the scale is squared at each step: 5² → 5⁴ → 5⁸ → 5¹⁶. It is shown that this formula is the best quadratic formula for the level up to 5⁴: it is exact everywhere except for one compensating pair of misses (p = 15 and p = 17). The quadratic lattice of a level holds up to the basis 7 inclusive and breaks down right after it. The error of the formula splits into two superimposed tables: a smooth level correction and an oscillation which, in the explicit formula, is a sum of cosines over the zeros of the zeta function. The main result is a law of levels, checked on exact values of π(x) up to 3³² ≈ 1.9 · 10¹⁵: when the scale is squared, the relative error of the prime count is squared, and the error itself is inverse to the linear scale p = √x obtained from the difference of squares: ε · p stays of order one at all checked steps. The law holding at all steps is equivalent to the Riemann hypothesis (von Koch, 1901). The author puts forward the hypothesis that the self-similarity of the ladder may become a route to its proof: for this one must show that the step structure itself does not allow ε · p to grow faster than a power of the logarithm. This step is named but not taken. The method may become the basis for an exact count of prime density by levels without the exponential and the logarithm in the level formula. Section 7 gives a geometric reading for a reader without mathematical training: why the basis of the model is 2, 3, 5, 7, how the seam 8–9 links the linear and the quadratic levels, why the centres of the seam differ by exactly ¼ and how π arises from all the differences together, where zero is on the arrow and why the whole arrow projects into one circle. The similarity with the construction of the Birth of Dimensions model is shown. Section 8 shows that the accumulated mismatch over the seams is Euler's sine at one half (π), while accumulation over the primes gives γ (Mertens); that the error of the prime count at a step is of the order of the square root of the mismatch of the frame; and that the transfer of the observer changes nothing if and only if all zeros lie on the axis 1/2 — this is the Hilbert — Pólya programme. Each seam is a right triangle in a circle: the centre along the line is the radius, the centre on the circle the cosine, the hole the sine, and sin² + cos² = 1. The author believes that this work can become a proof of the Riemann hypothesis; the missing step is to show that the unity of the process makes the transfer of the observer a symmetry. The work is laid out as a programme of proof: the missing step is formulated as a target statement resting on the birth of the arrow — a pure projection from one unit, the product over the primes. The missing step is also written as a statement about positivity: from Mertens' square 2(1 + cos θ)², which pushes the zeros away from 1, to the square of Weil's energy, which must hold them on ½ and forbid pairs of zeros on opposite sides of the circle. The work rests on classical results — Pell–Lagrange, Legendre's sieve, the explicit formula of Riemann and von Mangoldt — and proposes a new linking of them: the geometry of the seam as a model of the process linking the primes. The author's answer to Riemann's question is geometric: on each range chosen in a definite way, the process of the link of the primes is seen as the unit circle and a sinusoid around it; for his work the author regards this answer as a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, and what in it is accepted as an initial prin

summary: This dataset provides time-domain OpenFAST simulation results for the NREL 5-MW reference wind turbine mounted on the OC4-DeepCwind semisubmersible floating platform. Version 2.0.1 is a documentation, packaging and reproducibility-evidence correction. The numerical dataset is unchanged from version 2.0.0: it contains 256 Sea-State Groups and 1,280 simulation realisations, comprising the original population of 123 groups / 615 realisations and an extension of 133 groups / 665 realisations. Every group contains five wind-speed cases at 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11 m/s. The 32 ZIP archives containing the raw OpenFAST time histories are unchanged. Qualification follows explicit and orthogonal criteria for physical-domain membership and numerical-record integrity. The combined inventory contains 175 Class A groups, 16 Class B groups and 65 Class C groups. Of the 1,280 realisations, 1,279 pass all mandatory C3 checks. The retained realisation G0013-V08 is shorter than the project-specific full-record completeness threshold of 300 Tp; its parent group also independently lies outside the adopted physical domain. The duration criterion is evaluated on the available record from t=0 and does not imply that an initial transient was removed. Version 2.0.1: synchronises the repository documentation with the complete 256-group version-2.0 domain described by the revised Data in Brief article; documents that the archived first-order wave-frequency band is 0.314159–1.570796 rad/s and supplies an explicit table of the 48 groups with nominal Tp <= 4 s, whose requested spectral peak lies above or at the upper cutoff; distinguishes the ROSCO 2.10.1 run-time banner from the ROSCO 2.7.0 tuning-file header; stages byte-identical controller input and rotor-performance-table copies in the worked OpenFAST case directory so that the archived relative paths resolve without changing any controller value; adds the completed representative replay and time-step-sensitivity workflow for Class A case G0195-V07, including scripts, compact evidence, hashes and a reviewed assessment; adds a deterministic finite-record sensitivity analysis over all 27 eligible Class A, C3-valid groups and 81 runs at Tp = 2, 3, 4, 7 or 9 s and V = 7, 9 and 11 m/s. Relative to the 300 Tp mean generated power, the complete-population median absolute differences are 0.1352% at 200 Tp and 0.0662% at 250 Tp; maxima are 0.8091% and 0.3195%, with all runs below 1% and 0.5%, respectively; reconciles all 665 extension manifest paths against the central directories of the 16 unchanged extension archives: 648 exact matches, 16 decimal wind-suffix corrections and one documented G0181 seed-truncation filename match, with zero unresolved paths. For G0195-V07, the exact-step replay reproduced all eight audited archived channels to the precision stored in the output files over 216,001 aligned samples from 300 to 3,000 s. In the half-step comparison, absolute relative differences in response-channel means were below 0.006%, and the largest range-normalised RMSE was 0.877%. These results are a representative reproducibility and time-step-sensitivity check; they are not a campaign-wide convergence study or experimental/physical validation. The release includes OpenFAST configurations, persistent Group and Realisation identifiers, entity and qualification tables, development and frozen hold-out partitions, provenance documentation, loading and validation code, the short-period wave-band table, complete finite-record sensitivity tables, extension archive-member reconciliation tables, and the compact representative replay evidence. summary: This dataset provides time-domain OpenFAST simulation results for the NREL 5-MW reference wind turbine mounted on the OC4-DeepCwind semisubmersible floating platform. Version 2.0.1 is a documentation, packaging and reproducibility-evidence correction. The numerical dataset is unchanged from version 2.0.0: it contains 256 Sea-State Groups and 1,280 simulation realisations, comprising the original population of 123 groups / 615 realisations and an extension of 133 groups / 665 realisations. Every group contains five wind-speed cases at 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11 m/s. The 32 ZIP archives containing the raw OpenFAST time histories are unchanged. Qualification follows explicit and orthogonal criteria for physical-domain membership and numerical-record integrity. The combined inventory contains 175 Class A groups, 16 Class B groups and 65 Class C groups. Of the 1,280 realisations, 1,279 pass all mandatory C3 checks. The retained realisation G0013-V08 is shorter than the project-specific full-record completeness threshold of 300 Tp; its parent group also independently lies outside the adopted physical domain. The duration criterion is evaluated on the available record from t=0 and does not imply that an initial transient was removed. Version 2.0.1: synchronises the repository documentation with the complete 256-group version-2.0 domain described by the revised Data in Brief article; documents that the archived first-order wave-frequency band is 0.314159–1.570796 rad/s and supplies an explicit table of the 48 groups with nominal Tp <= 4 s, whose requested spectral peak lies above or at the upper cutoff; distinguishes the ROSCO 2.10.1 run-time banner from the ROSCO 2.7.0 tuning-file header; stages byte-identical controller input and rotor-performance-table copies in the worked OpenFAST case directory so that the archived relative paths resolve without changing any controller value; adds the completed representative replay and time-step-sensitivity workflow for Class A case G0195-V07, including scripts, compact evidence, hashes and a reviewed assessment; adds a deterministic finite-record sensitivity analysis over all 27 eligible Class A, C3-valid groups and 81 runs at Tp = 2, 3, 4, 7 or 9 s and V = 7, 9 and 11 m/s. These results are a representative reproducibility and time-step-sensitivity check; they are not a campaign-wide convergence study or experimental/physical validation. summary: The application of the FAIR Principles to digital research objects is near ubiquitous with endorsement by funders, publishers, and research organizations worldwide. At the national level in the UK, this is demonstrated by the draft UKRI Research Data Policy which puts an increased emphasis on FAIR compliance; the latest version of the UKRIO Code of Practice which strengthens expectations around data management and sharing, aligned with the FAIR Principles; the UKRI AI Research and Innovation Strategic Framework , and the UK DSIT AI for Science Strategy policy paper, which emphasise the importance of ensuring that data generated through UKRI-funded research aligns with FAIR to support a modernised, AI-ready data environment. Across the research landscape, statements such as “our repository enables FAIR data” or “this dataset meets the FAIR principles” are increasingly common. Yet, these claims are often difficult to interpret or trust, despite numerous tools having been implemented in the decade since the FAIR principles were launched. As this EOSC report has highlighted, the diversity of assessment approaches, many of them opaque or tool-specific, makes it hard to know what is really being measured, how rigorously, and against which definition(s) of FAIR. The FAIR Institutional Repository Metrics (FIRM) project was established in response to this challenge, with the first phase running from March to August 2026. Led by FAIRsharing and the Oxford University Research Archive (ORA) in collaboration with the UK Reproducibility Network (UKRN) , FIRM is a collaborative initiative to define and test a common FAIR compliance process for institutional repositories participating in the UKRN Open Research Programme. The participating repositories were generalist institutional repositories, supporting research datasets across a wide range of disciplines and research contexts. FIRM builds on the FAIR assessment work undertaken at the University of Oxford for ORA, moving from a single-repository interpretation towards a shared community benchmark. The resulting FAIR Benchmark for Institutional Repository Datasets provides a structured, transparent and reusable framework for assessing dataset metadata against the FAIR Principles. It covers both datasets deposited within an institutional repository and datasets held in external repositories but referenced or catalogued through it.  The FAIR compliance enabled by this benchmark uses a transparent procedure that shifts the focus from assessment to assistance, initially developed by the EOSC OSTrails project, of which the FAIRsharing team is a part. Targeted at developers and technical research support staff, this OSTrails Assessment Interoperability Framework (Assess-IF) provides ‘components’ that enable the definition of what FAIR means in a given context, how it should be measured, and how results should be weighted, interpreted, and potentially improved. FAIRsharing’s rich, manually curated metadata on standards, databases, and policies provide supporting context for the compliance and assistance process. The benchmark translates the high-level FAIR Principles into a set of concrete interpretations for institutional repository datasets covering identifiers, discovery metadata, links between metadata and data, searchability, access protocols, machine-readable metadata, FAIR vocabularies, relationships among research objects, licensing, provenance and recognised standards. The benchmark distinguishes between characteristics delivered through repository infrastructure or policy and those dependent on the metadata supplied for an individual record. This makes it possible to identify where FAIR compliance is effectively provided by the repository and where researchers or repository submission workflows have a role to play. A key contribution of FIRM is alignment. Participating institutions have considered how existing generic FAIR metrics apply to th

summary: Software and reproducibility archive accompanying the author-review manuscript “Beyond Prediction Accuracy: Local-Slope Robustness in Takagi–Sugeno Fuzzy Models of Airfoil Self-Noise.” The IEEE Access manuscript has not been accepted or published; this DOI will identify the research archive, not the article. The NASA/UCI coefficient-sign certificate uses 1,503 airfoil self-noise observations in 106 operating groups. Selected TSK ridge has 4.166475 dB equal-configuration RMSE and Extra Trees has 2.381 dB. With a 0.1 dB maximum training-prediction change and 1% ridge-objective allowance, 403 of 510 local slope signs are protected and 107 admit strict reversal. A separate 1 dB plus 1% contextual sensitivity gives 135 protected and 375 strict reversals. Neither threshold is a calibrated per-row prediction interval. The R19 Southampton leave-one-geometry-out evaluation has 343 source-normalized rows, 38 spectra and seven geometries; equal-geometry normalized RMSE is 0.059396 for TSK and 0.047839 for Extra Trees. It does not establish absolute-SPL transfer. The UCI concrete source/split sensitivity is exploratory and supports no causal physical conclusion. This deposit contains the two previously SHA-verified EP10 public research ZIPs, 40 task ZIPs of newly reconstructed bootstrap states and audit journals, a SHA-256 manifest, standalone integrity verifier, completion certificate, independent QA record, environment specification and rights/provenance notices. The 40 task archives total 773,361,055 bytes and document 28,000 attempts, 27,998 newly replayed fitted states and two reproduced FCM fitting failures. The original historical fitted-state bytes and first October 2026 UCI download bytes remain unavailable. The new state files must not be described as recovered originals. A full historical-array numerical comparison requires reference arrays outside this public bundle; the included verifier checks all released state hashes, journals, CRCs and failure identities using public files alone. MIT applies to original project code authorized by its rights holders; CC BY 4.0 applies to original authored documentation and derived records authorized by their rights holders. NASA/UCI, Southampton and Concrete source data retain upstream attribution and licence terms. Third-party publisher materials, Bristol raw HDF5, confidential correspondence, reviewer letters and credentials are excluded. No external research funding was received. See LICENSE_SCOPE.md and README_RELEASE.md for component-level scope and executable instructions.

summary: > This dataset supports a study of the spatial settings of the PC horror games that reached the largest audiences on Steam between 2015 and 2025. Unlike the ownership-only horror census, it measures exposure in three ways side by side: estimated owners (SteamSpy), measured play hours January 2015 – December 2025 (steamcharts.com) and total user reviews. A game enters the sample if it has at least one million owners, or is among the top 100 by play hours or by reviews. > > The frame is every game in the Steam store with the tag Horror, Psychological Horror, Survival Horror or Lovecraftian (12,798 games). After restricting to releases 2015–2025, requiring a horror tag among a game's five most-voted tags and excluding 13 games whose horror tag is a joke tag, the sample contains 131 games; 30 of them enter through play hours or reviews alone. > > Each game has draft codes for its playable environments (domestic, institutional, industrial, infrastructural, natural, urban, maritime, liminal), the original function and state of its main space, and seven ecological and infrastructural markers (decay, contamination, extraction, climate stress, resource scarcity, infrastructure failure, corporate or institutional control). The codebook gives the definitions and rules. > > Version 0.1 is preliminary: the exposure data are complete, but the setting codes are unverified drafts with confidence ratings. Hour-weighted results depend heavily on Dead by Daylight (31 % of all play hours). Data retrieved 23 November 2026. Prepared for the talk "Spatial Settings in High-Exposure Horror Games" (Geographies of Horror).

summary: Dataset and Python Pipeline (Version 2.0): Maize Yield Prediction from Tillage Operations and Soil Properties Version 2.0 Update: Updated to include nested season-block ANOVA ( Season fixed, Block nested within Season ), fully nested cross-validation schemes (plot-grouped 5-fold CV, leave-one-block-out, and season-wise validation), and predictor-subset comparisons (operational vs. soil variables) . This repository provides the experimental dataset ( Xplow_720samples.xlsx ) and reproducible Python pipeline ( Cod_v2.py ) for the study: "Neural-Network Prediction of Maize Yield from Tillage Operations and Soil Properties: Plot-Grouped Validation" . Dataset: 720 observations from 240 plots (3 subsamples/plot; 4 blocks/season across 2 seasons) on a saline clay Entisol in southern Iraq, evaluating five tillage systems ( CT , CTr , RT , RTr , MT ), two forward speeds ( 0.97 , 1.53 m s⁻¹ ), three depths ( 150 , 225 , 300 mm ), flowering-stage soil properties ( PR , BD , porosity, EC1:1 , MWD , Ks ), and maize grain yield ( t ha⁻¹ ). Pipeline Stages ( python Cod_v2.py --stage <name> ): stats : Nested Season/Block ANOVA, Tukey HSD, Kruskal–Wallis, Spearman correlations, and VIF . tune : 500-trial Optuna Bayesian optimization on plot-grouped splits . eval : PyTorch MLP training, 10,000 cluster-bootstrap CIs, baseline comparisons ( MLR , Ridge , SVR , RF , GBM , DNN ), nested 5-fold CV, LOBO , season-wise validation, and feature-group comparisons . xai : Permutation importance, SHAP ( KernelExplainer ), sensitivity coefficients, and residual diagnostics . block : Joint block-wise permutation importance . figs : Automated export of publication-grade figures (300 DPI) .
title: Data and Python Pipeline for Maize Grain Yield Prediction from Tillage and Soil Properties

summary: Derived data for the article "Where Does Single-Smartphone Biomechanics Lose Accuracy? A Matched Benchmark of Human Mesh Recovery Front Ends" (Z. Shi, manuscript submitted to Sensors, 2026). For each of four single-smartphone systems (InstantHMR, SAM 3D Body, HSMR, and OpenCap Monocular re-run with its released code) and each participant of the public OpenCap LabValidation dataset (nine participants, 45-degree iPhone view), the files contain the virtual-marker trajectories after the OpenCap Monocular-style alignment (TRC; the input to inverse kinematics), the scaled OpenSim models (LaiUhlrich2022), and the inverse-kinematics solutions (MOT) with their marker errors (STO). Re-solving inverse kinematics from these marker files with the OpenCap Monocular IK setup reproduced every participant's mean absolute error reported in the article within 0.003 degrees. Units: marker positions in metres, joint angles in degrees, time in seconds on the motion-capture time base. README.md describes the folder structure. No videos, images, or motion-capture data of the original dataset are included; download those from https://simtk.org/projects/opencap. Analysis code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24478998
title: Derived marker trajectories, scaled OpenSim models and inverse-kinematics solutions for: Where Does Single-Smartphone Biomechanics Lose Accuracy?

summary: Project-based learning (PjBL) is promoted as an approach to student-centred higher education, yet learning outcomes depend on how projects, feedback and assessment are designed. Objective: This critical narrative review synthesizes international research on relationships between PjBL, student engagement and higher-order learning, and proposes an actionable implementation framework. Methods: Twenty influential theoretical, review and empirical publications were purposively examined using a transparent thematic matrix covering learning outcomes, engagement mechanisms, assessment and limitations. Results: The literature associates well-supported PjBL with authentic problem solving, collaboration and motivation; however, estimates vary across contexts and most studies have methodological constraints. A frequently neglected dimension is the quality of student artifacts and direct measures of learning. Implications: Effective implementation requires a real-world driving question, structured milestones, inclusive team processes, formative feedback and individual accountability. Conclusion: PjBL should be evaluated as a designed instructional system rather than as an undifferentiated intervention. Longitudinal, controlled studies using multiple outcome measures are needed.
tags: project-based learning; student engagement; higher education; active learning; collaborative learning; formative assessment; instructional design.

summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/24481071 . ## Summary This paper presents a wearable navigation aid for visually impaired people. An ESP32 camera on the glasses captures the scene; a YOLO-World detection module localizes objects on a 2×3 spatial grid; the detections are encoded into a structured text prompt; GPT-4o, explicitly described as cloud-based language reasoning, converts the prompt into high-level navigation commands ("left", "right", "forward", "stop"); and temple-mounted actuators render these commands as haptic patterns through a five-bar linkage. Three studies are reported: recognition of 13 haptic patterns by 13 participants (81.3% average), path following in a motion-capture room by 6 participants using haptic cues generated from ground-truth position, and an offline comparison of GPT-4o's navigation decisions against human judgment in three corridor scenarios (decision accuracies of 91.8%, 84.6% and 81.5% for open space, static and dynamic obstacles). ## Strengths - The interaction channel is well chosen. Audio guidance competes with the environmental hearing that blind pedestrians rely on for orientation; temple-mounted haptics leave the ears free and the hands unoccupied. This is a real design merit, not a novelty for its own sake. - The pipeline design is sensible: the language model consumes a structured text summary of detections rather than raw images, which keeps prompts small and the module boundaries clean. - The haptic pattern study is reported with a full confusion matrix and inferential statistics, including the patterns users actually confuse (e.g. right tap at 0.65). - The authors consistently scope their claims to "controlled environments" and themselves name responsiveness as future work. The framing is honest in places; the concerns below are about where the wording outruns even that framing. ## Major concerns 1. "Real-time" is claimed throughout, but no latency is ever measured. The abstract, the system description and the Figure 1 caption all promise real-time guidance, yet the paper contains no end-to-end latency figure of any kind: no camera-to-feedback delay, no cloud round-trip time, no pipeline update rate. The word "latency" appears exactly once, in the introduction, criticizing prior speech-based systems for failing to provide "low-latency, embodied feedback". The only timing quantity measured for the authors' own system is the haptic pattern execution time of 1.25 s, which the paper itself notes "limited responsiveness during rapid movements"; optimizing response times is deferred to future work. For a device whose output directs a walking blind user, this is not a detail: at a typical walking speed the user covers well over a meter during a single cloud round trip plus a 1.25 s pattern playback, and a late "stop" is worse than no "stop". Please measure and report end-to-end latency (scene change to haptic onset), including the GPT-4o round trip and the query rate, or remove "real-time" from the claims. 2. No visually impaired person has used the system, and the integrated system has never been used for navigation at all. Both human studies recruited participants "with normal sensorimotor function" (13 and 6 participants respectively). More importantly, the studies evaluate the components separately, never the system: in Study 2, the haptic cues are generated from VICON ground-truth positions along predefined paths, so neither the camera pipeline nor GPT-4o is in the loop; Study 3 is an offline, photo-based test in which nobody walks. The abstract's conclusion that the system "can deliver reliable navigation support in controlled environments" therefore rests on a haptic display tested in sighted users, plus an offline agreement score. summary: Snapshot of the turboquant-pro repository at commit 5389c05, the state submitted with the PVLDB paper "Routed Recall Does Not Degrade at a Trillion Rows [Experiment, Analysis & Benchmark]". It carries the corpus generator and seeds, the build, exact-scan, routed, score and metadata scripts and the pool driver under benchmarks/fleet/; the record of the trillion-row runs under benchmarks/fleet/record/1t/ (pool state files, every driver log, the pilot logs, and the score logs with every per-server search time) and of the regenerated-index run under benchmarks/fleet/record/1trg/; the scripts that compute the figures and tables under paper/pvldb1t/figdata/; the Lean 4 development paper/pvldb1t/lean/; and the paper's LaTeX source. paper/pvldb1t/README.md maps every table and figure to its record files and scripts. The run's shared-volume data and non-member partials are in the companion data record, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23608434.

It carries the corpus generator and seeds, the build, exact-scan, routed, score and metadata scripts and the pool driver under benchmarks/fleet/; the record of the trillion-row runs under benchmarks/fleet/record/1t/ (pool state files, every driver log, the pilot logs, and the score logs with every per-server search time) and of the regenerated-index run under benchmarks/fleet/record/1trg/; the scripts that compute the figures and tables under paper/pvldb1t/figdata/; the Lean 4 development paper/pvldb1t/lean/; and the paper's LaTeX source. paper/pvldb1t/README.md maps every table and figure to its record files and scripts. The run's shared-volume data and non-member partials are in the companion data record, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23608434.

summary: Record of a measurement of routed inverted-file search over a sharded index of one trillion 4-bit quantized vectors (500 servers of two billion rows, 24 TB), built and measured on the National Research Platform's Nautilus cluster. This is the data companion to the code and record snapshot of the turboquant-pro repository (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23608470) and to the paper "Routed Recall Does Not Degrade at a Trillion Rows [Experiment, Analysis & Benchmark]", under submission to PVLDB. shared-fleet-20260929.tar.gz (sha256 02f27a4cd734af4cb224747bb812845537ad15e12bac9c2e8ee38b9372d86d75): the shared volume of the run as of 2026-09-29, 3814 files: the bootstrap shard with its cell membership and offsets, and the 2048-cell coarse quantizer (centroids and radii); per-server reference (exact scan) and routed top-10 partials at every scale point (1e8, 1e10, 1e11, 1e12 rows) and probe width; cell histograms; the rerank-bound inputs and result; the nested-scale result; the analysis outputs. shared-fleet-20260929.manifest.json lists every member with its sha256. nonmember-1tnm-partials-20261002.tar.gz (sha256 9b6d854a4ff4008b602bc26d60771a6f351389a72a31d6f515a719359bc9fd4c): run tag 1tnm, 100 queries drawn under seeds no corpus shard uses (shards 200000, 250000, 300000, 350000): the 500 reference partials, the 500 routed partials at 32 and at 128 probes, the query file, the run summary, the 500 per-volume index checksum manifests, and SHA256SUMS over 2002 files. Deterministic tarball (names sorted, mtime 2026-10-02 00:00 UTC, owner 0, gzip -n -9). The index itself (500 volumes) is not included; it is a function of the corpus seeds and the code, and a rebuild can be checked file by file against the checksum manifests.

summary: Changes for v1.1.1: Uncertainty calculation fixes, other minor fixes Code for snow freshwater flux calculation, including output data; refer to README.md for additional information and full references. Archived from GitHub. Makes use of the following datasets: Sea ice fluxes from the RADARSAT Constellation Mission and Sentinel-1 (Howell et al., 2022): https://catalogue.ec.gc.ca/geonetwork/srv/api/records/09ab22c4-e211-4d23-afe6-9e7aa6831c62 Ice volume flux calculated in the above using version 2.0 of the Landy et al. (2022) year-round sea ice thickness data (Landy et al., 2026): https://data.npolar.no/dataset/6581f94e-d88d-4237-a555-712d19b1e527 Snow datasets used (article references + dataset doi): NESOSIM: NASA Eulerian Snow On Sea Ice Model, v1.1 (Petty et al., 2018): https://zenodo.org/records/18273881 SnowModel-LG: Lagrangian Snow Distributions for Sea Ice Applications, version 1 (Liston et al., 2020; Stroeve et al., 2020): https://nsidc.org/data/nsidc-0758/versions/1 5VLSTM: 25 km resolution snow depth on Arctic sea ice dataset (2012-2020) (Li et al., 2022): https://data.tpdc.ac.cn/zh-hans/data/8b4b5f67-ee01-45ee-96a6-db8f712a2e0c LEGOS: Multi-frequency altimetry snow depth product over Arctic sea ice (Carret et al., 2025): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14000765 NaRRS: Nadir Radiometer and Radar Synergy for Arctic Snow Depth and Sea Ice Thickness Retrieval (Nelson et al., 2026): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17942492 Sea ice age: EASE-Grid Sea Ice Age, Version 4 (Tschudi et al., 2019): https://doi.org/10.5067/UTAV7490FEPB Snow salinity: From observational data from Nandan et al. (2017): https://doi.org/10.1002/2017GL074506

summary: This release adds a combined Micro-C QC report and a local beta workflow for shallow single-cell RNA libraries. Compare fragment sizes, Pairtools categories, ligation structure and inferred MNase fragment sizes across sublibraries. The report includes separate genomic block and insert-length figures, a downloadable SVG overview and expandable per-library detail. Micro-C example Follow each sublibrary across plots with a consistent, brighter palette. Reference species have their own fixed colors. Chromatin size and genomic profiles now have their own report card. Chromatin example Run shallow single-cell RNA QC locally for supported 10x Chromium, MGI C4 and Parse Evercode layouts. Reports summarize barcode evidence, cDNA yield and observed gene-assigned molecules. scRNA QC guide Portal operators can configure a lower memory reservation for preparation and reporting. The worker reserves additional memory for alignment and releases it when that phase finishes. Full changelog
title: Shall-We-Dance/ONT-LibQC: ONT-LibQC v1.2.0

summary: Financial documents combine narrative disclosures, accounting metrics, corporate structures, management commentary, and time-dependent facts, making them difficult to represent using conventional chunk-based retrieval-augmented generation systems. This paper presents an auditable, schema-driven methodology for constructing temporal financial knowledge graphs from page-delimited documents parsed using a general purpose document intelligence service. Overlapping document windows undergo phased large language model extraction of structural entities, quantitative observations, and domain-specific relationships. Candidate graph elements are validated against predefined schemas and consolidated through scope-aware exact, normalized, fuzzy, embedding-based, and LLM-assisted entity resolution. Temporal merge constraints, deterministic edge deduplication, conflict-aware property management, and fine-grained provenance preserve issuer identity, reporting-period validity, and traceability to source evidence. The contributions of this work comprise the proposed methodology for financial knowledge graph construction, the creation of an evidence-grounded temporal knowledge graph from heterogeneous financial documents, and an intrinsic framework for evaluating the quality of the resulting graph. The evaluation framework assesses seven weighted dimensions, two hard validation gates, and structural diagnostics. By separating graph-quality assessment from downstream retrieval and answer generation, the framework supports systematic diagnosis and iterative refinement of the constructed graph.
title: Auditable Financial Knowledge Graphs: Schema-Driven Construction and Intrinsic Quality Evaluation

summary: We present ChildAI-Gov, an explainable AI system for assessing whether education-technology (EdTech) policies respect children's digital rights. Generative AI is reaching children's education faster than its governance can keep pace, yet checking a tool against children's rights remains manual, expert-dependent, and slow. We propose the Child Rights Impact Score (CRIS), an evidence-linked measure across five dimensions: safety, privacy, transparency, autonomy, and non-discrimination. ChildAI-Gov reads an EdTech tool's privacy or AI policy and scores each dimension by combining a large-language-model judgement (gpt-4o-mini) with a deterministic rule check. A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) component grounds every score in the governing provisions, retrieved from a curated knowledge base of children's rights frameworks (the EU AI Act, UNICEF guidance, and others), so each score is tied to the evidence behind it and an auditor can trace which provision it rests on. We also construct AIPolicy-EdTech, a dataset of 57 real EdTech policies. On it, the five dimensions cohered as a single measure (Cronbach's alpha = 0.79), and grounding made scoring stricter while preserving rankings; an ungrounded baseline was far more lenient, passing nearly half the policies where ChildAI-Gov passed none. It offers evidence-linked decision support on documented commitments, not observation of real-world behaviour or determinations of legal compliance.
title: ChildAI-Gov: An Evidence-Linked AI System for Assessing EdTech Policies Against Children's Digital Rights

summary: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system answers questions using passages it retrieves from a knowledge base, so users must trust that knowledge base. We study an attacker who quietly edits existing passages by swapping words for synonyms (PWWS, TextFooler) in a cybersecurity RAG system built from MITRE ATT&CK and CAPEC. Using a reviewed 44-question benchmark, repeated paired runs and a control corpus in which only the layout changes, we find that poisoning lowers judged answer correctness from 0.714 to 0.555. The damage comes mostly from lost evidence and refusals, not from false statements. To find the edited passages, we use relative entropy. Comparing a whole passage with normal text is a weak signal. Still, one term of the relative entropy, the log-ratio between a word and its most probable synonym, works well: with a small language model as the reference, it reaches an AUROC of 0.95 and stays near chance on the control. Used as a retrieval filter, it halves how often edited text reaches the generator, and an attacker who must keep each passage as probable under the language model fails on all 57 sections it tries. Filtering does not restore correctness, because the edited passage is usually the one that held the answer. We therefore add a runtime monitor that checks each answer against trusted MITRE STIX data and remembers the passages it rejects. On its own, it reduces exposure to edited text from 0.41 to 0.26; when it may add the trusted MITRE entry as a source, correctness rises to 0.786. We report the costs and failure cases of every defence alongside its gains.
title: Detecting Word-Substitution Poisoning of a RAG Knowledge Base with Relative Entropy and Runtime Verification
